The IMSR is a study of the interaction between the Earth's surface and the ocean. It is an ongoing project, in which we seek to answer questions about how the oceans are affected by human activities on land, sea, and air.
The main focus is on the oceanic ecosystem and how it interacts with its terrestrial environment (e.g., marine ecosystems, ecosystems in coastal areas). This includes changes in land use (agricultural expansion and mining) as well as changes in climate conditions such as increased salinity.
In addition, this study will explore the interplay between two physical mechanisms - topography and temperature - that may be responsible for the observed variations in ocean currents. The first involves the measurement of global sea level rise caused by warming due to greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel burning. This is one of the most difficult aspects of the science of climate change to predict and understand. The second involves the study of the impact of regional climate variability on water quality, including the effect of global sea level rise on aquatic ecosystems.

- The study of the causes of disease is called pathology. A cause may be external or internal. Internal causes are those that can be easily detected in the body by examining the blood, urine, feces, and stool of an infected person. The causes may be contagious, toxic, or infectious (e.g., viruses). Internal causes include infection with bacteria or fungus (such as fungi) or exposure to certain chemicals (including formaldehyde, chlorine, or other toxic substances). There are also many types of diseases that may affect different organs. In addition, some people have very specific genetic disorders that make them susceptible to a particular type of disease.
The symptoms depend on which part of the body is affected. For example, chronic pain and muscle weakness may cause damage to the spinal cord. Sometimes these problems go away quickly without treatment. Other times they get worse over time. Symptoms may appear suddenly, such as a sore throat, fever, chills, headache, nausea, vomiting, and/or sweating. People who suffer from acute inflammation may develop a feeling of discomfort when walking or standing for long periods of time. Some people may have joint aches and pains, fever, fatigue, and feelings of weakness.

Kowalski has the opportunity to lead an expedition in her native island of Palau to study and record coral reef life.
The corals are incredibly important for our planet because they provide food and shelter for countless species that live there. In fact, more than half of all corals have been destroyed by coral bleaching events caused by rising global temperatures. Coral reefs provide many benefits: They prevent erosion; provide habitat for fish and birds; filter harmful pollutants from the air; protect coastlines from storms and tsunamis.
Unfortunately, the damage done to coral reefs is far greater than we can imagine. Corals are so fragile, it’s almost impossible to survive them without killing them.
But we must not let this happen. Instead, we need to create a healthy ecosystem at home on our shores!
Sacred corals like the St Paul’s Star (Stellaria media) and the Red-ringed (Stella sinensis) species are part of the world’s most threatened ecosystems. These creatures help maintain the health of the sea and reefs around us. Their services include filtering toxic chemicals, producing oxygen, recycling nutrients, and providing shelter for marine mammals. We also depend on these corals for their own survival.
